hook: This one opens before the report does: a warning screen and a short, melancholy passage you are asked to get through first. Read everything on the page, including the parts that don't look like they belong to the article. The file is about things vanishing, and it uses the page itself to make that feel personal.
whyItMatters: SCP-3309 sits in the wiki's metafiction tradition, where both the joke and the horror depend on the reader knowing the Foundation is a collaborative writing site. Its central idea is pointed: anomalies disappear when their files read like weak, overwritten drafts, so the community's own quality standards become a physical force. An Ethics Committee vote then turns that force into the hinge of the story.
thingsToNotice:
Look closely at the list of criteria: overbuilt titanium cells, apocalyptic stakes with no real detail, sloppy formatting. It is a checklist of complaints anyone who has read many rejected drafts will recognise, and the Foundation turns it into a weapon after winning approval by a single vote. The test on the Arizona anomaly is staged as a deliberately bad rewrite, a neat bit of self-parody.

Then the narration starts losing people. Smalls' note drifts from routine to dread, colleagues stop remembering he existed, and the final section becomes a mock discussion thread where staff dismiss his pleas as forum roleplay and open a deletion vote. Those fake comments are the actual ending, so don't skip them.
